name: Colorist
description: Samples the dominant colour of frames across a video and renders them as a vertical-stripe movie barcode, stored beside the media and shown at the foot of the detail page.

versions.changelog: The current build. Everything below, plus a settings page that reads like the rest of the dashboard: the action buttons render as Jellyfin buttons rather than bare browser ones, the delete button stays an ordinary button until you arm it and then says what the next click will do, and the tab bar carries a baseline so the panel you are looking at is underlined. Those buttons had never rendered correctly on any earlier release. Their styling turns on a class the dashboard adds at runtime through a custom-elements API that browsers have since removed, which survives only through a polyfill and only for the elements it happens to see, so the page now carries that class itself instead of hoping.

The top of the run-logging era, and the last build before the settings page was restyled. Every run writes a log and the Run tab shows the live one: a progress bar that updates every two seconds with what is being sampled, how far through the run is, how many items a minute it is getting through and how long is left. The estimate is built from measured throughput rather than an average item duration, so a run that changes pace crossing from feature films into half-hour episodes is followed rather than averaged away, and a run stalled on one enormous file shows a growing estimate instead of counting down through a hang. Under it, recent runs are listed newest first; open one to see every item it touched, with the outcome, the time taken, the frames sampled and the stripes they became, the crop applied, any HDR conversion, whether the barcode landed beside the media or in the plugin data directory, and the reason for anything that failed. The list stays where you scrolled it rather than snapping to the top on every refresh. A slider sets the share of the processors a run may take, defaulting to 25 percent, which is what the old fixed rule worked out to, and the page says what that resolves to on your server; typing an explicit number of items at once still overrides it. Run history recorded by older versions is renamed and reordered the first time the list is shown, so it sorts by when each run started rather than by when its file was last written, and a run you cancel is recorded as cancelled rather than failed. Stop here if you want the run tooling and none of the cosmetic work above it, and expect the action buttons on the settings page to render as plain browser buttons: that is fixed in 0.3.4.0 and in nothing below it.

Everything before run logs, and the oldest build worth installing. Barcodes are stored as the colours that were sampled rather than as a picture of them — a small JSON sidecar of about 6 KB per item, one packed hex triplet per stripe — and the detail page draws the strip in the browser, so stripe blending and display height become a page reload instead of another ffmpeg pass over the whole library. Blended strips are interpolated perceptually in Oklab rather than through the dark seam plain sRGB blending leaves at every transition. The strip spans the full width of the detail page and ends flush with its foot, and it is fetched with a real Authorization header, so no access token travels in a URL. A Delete Barcodes task and a button on the settings page remove what Colorist has written from library folders and from the plugin data directory, defaulting to clearing only the optional PNGs and keeping the colours. HDR and Dolby Vision are converted before their colours are measured, profile 5 through libplacebo, rather than being read as though they were SDR and coming out muted and grey; frame analysis is capped at the stripe count you asked for, instead of scaling and clustering every frame of a 4K film. Below this release barcodes are images with no colour data behind them and cannot be converted, so anything sampled by 0.1.x is sampled again on the next run — and below 0.1.1.0 the strip does not display at all.
